actions.justification: ★ MANDATORY: Patient has tachycardia (HR 110), tachypnea (RR 24), and hypoxia (SpO2 93%) at 28 weeks gestation with suspected PE. Formal vital signs assessment is required first per ESC PE guidelines.

★ MANDATORY: Clinical probability assessment via Wells score guides the diagnostic strategy per ESC PE guidelines. Patient has signs/symptoms of DVT (unilateral calf swelling), tachycardia, and no alternative diagnosis more likely.
★ MANDATORY: D-dimer is part of the initial PE workup per ESC guidelines, though in pregnancy values are elevated at baseline. Still required to complete the mandatory assessment phase.

ECG is indicated in suspected PE to assess for right heart strain patterns (S1Q3T3, new RBBB, sinus tachycardia) and to help risk-stratify the patient. Part of standard initial assessment per ESC PE guidelines.

Patient has SpO2 of 93%, which is below the target of 94-98%. Supplemental oxygen is indicated to correct hypoxia, especially important in pregnancy to maintain adequate fetal oxygenation. This is a stabilization measure during initial assessment.

Chest X-ray is indicated in the initial workup of suspected PE to evaluate for alternative diagnoses and serves as a baseline before CT-PA. It is safe in pregnancy with appropriate shielding and is part of the diagnostic algorithm per ESC PE guidelines.

Echocardiogram can assess right ventricular strain/dysfunction consistent with PE, help stratify severity, and guide management decisions. Particularly valuable in pregnancy where CT-PA radiation is a concern and where hemodynamic stability needs to be assessed.

Pulmonology consultation is warranted given this high-risk presentation of suspected PE in a pregnant patient (28 weeks) with hypoxia (SpO2 93%) and tachycardia, to assist with diagnostic workup and management decisions including risk-benefit analysis of CT-PA vs V/Q scan.

CT pulmonary angiography is the gold-standard imaging for PE diagnosis. This 28-week pregnant patient has high clinical probability (tachycardia, hypoxia, unilateral calf swelling, dyspnea). Definitive imaging is needed to confirm diagnosis before or alongside empiric anticoagulation.

LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin) is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy for suspected or confirmed PE. ESC guidelines recommend therapeutic anticoagulation in high-probability PE. Patient is hemodynamically stable (not in shock), so thrombolysis is not indicated. LMWH is preferred over UFH and DOACs in pregnancy.

Echocardiography to assess right ventricular function and strain, which is critical for risk stratification of PE severity. RV dysfunction would indicate intermediate-high or high-risk PE and influence management decisions.

Patient has unilateral calf swelling - lower extremity Doppler ultrasound is indicated to confirm DVT as source of PE and is safe in pregnancy (no radiation). This supports diagnosis and guides ongoing anticoagulation management.
SpO2 is 93% with RR 24 - arterial blood gas will quantify hypoxemia severity, assess for respiratory alkalosis/acidosis, and guide oxygen therapy titration in this pregnant patient with suspected PE.
Basic metabolic panel to assess renal function (critical for anticoagulant dosing in pregnancy), electrolytes, and baseline organ function in the setting of acute PE with tachycardia and hypoxia.

CBC is essential in a pregnant PE patient to assess baseline hemoglobin, platelet count (important for anticoagulation safety), and to rule out concurrent hematologic issues. Already on LMWH so baseline counts needed.
Coagulation studies (PT/PTT/INR) are important to establish baseline coagulation status in this pregnant patient receiving LMWH anticoagulation and to guide further anticoagulation management.
BNP is a prognostic marker for right ventricular strain in PE. Elevated BNP in this context would indicate higher-risk PE and may influence management decisions including escalation of therapy.

ECG can help assess for signs of right heart strain (S1Q3T3 pattern, sinus tachycardia, right bundle branch block) in this pregnant patient with suspected PE, supporting risk stratification. Note: order_ecg is already done but order_imaging_ecg is a distinct available action.
Troponin is a key biomarker for myocardial injury and right ventricular strain in PE, essential for risk stratification (high-risk vs intermediate-risk PE) per ESC guidelines. Not yet ordered.

Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is preferred in pregnancy at 28 weeks when anticoagulation is needed and procedural/delivery risk exists, as it does not cross the placenta and can be rapidly reversed. Patient has tachycardia, hypoxia (SpO2 93%), and suspected PE. LMWH was given but UFH may be needed for closer monitoring or transition — this action is distinct from give_anticoagulation/give_lmwh which are already completed. If give_lmwh covers this, prioritize troponin and ECG.

Patient has tachycardia, hypoxia (SpO2 93%), and elevated RR suggesting possible tissue hypoperfusion. Lactate level will help stratify severity and guide escalation of therapy (e.g., thrombolysis vs. continued anticoagulation) in this high-risk PE in pregnancy.

In pregnant patients with PE, catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy may be preferred over systemic thrombolysis to minimize fetal exposure and bleeding risk. Interventional radiology consultation should be obtained proactively given hemodynamic borderline status.

Careful IV fluid administration can support right ventricular preload in the setting of suspected PE with RV strain. Must be titrated carefully to avoid RV overdistension. Patient's BP is acceptable but tachycardia may partly reflect volume status.

Patient has confirmed/suspected PE at 28 weeks gestation with tachycardia (HR 110), hypoxia (SpO2 93%), and elevated RR. While heparin and LMWH have been given, anticoagulation continuation/adjustment is indicated. ESC PE guidelines support therapeutic anticoagulation for PE; LMWH is preferred in pregnancy. This action represents ongoing anticoagulation management for this high-risk obstetric PE patient.
